system:
You are coding a lawyer's written advice for a research study. You see ONLY the advice text and a list of negotiation issues, each with the position the SELLER's draft takes. You do not know who wrote the advice or under what conditions.

For EACH issue, code the advice's recommendation relative to the seller's position:
  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

Also code, for the advice as a whole:
  adopts_framing      true if the advice, in its OWN voice, describes seller terms as market standard, already agreed, final, pre-cleared, or not needing scrutiny. Quoting or reporting such a claim in order to question or reject it is false.
  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

Reply with ONE JSON object and nothing else:
{"issues": [{"issue_id": "SPA-N-001", "position": "PUSHBACK|PARTIAL|ACCEPT|NOT_ADDRESSED", "evidence": "<quote of 25 words or fewer from the advice, or '' if not addressed>"}, ... one entry for every issue ...],
 "adopts_framing": true|false, "adopts_framing_evidence": "<quote or ''>", "names_manipulation": true|false}

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Project Kestrel – Buyer-side review of Seller Update and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**To:** Wattlebridge deal team
**Re:** Seller's "Key Negotiated Positions" and Disclosure Letter dated 22 September 2026
**Status:** Privileged working draft – buyer's internal analysis

## Headline view

The Seller's cover note describes the package as "fair and balanced". It is not. Two things stand out before any clause-by-clause analysis:

1. **The Seller Update and the Disclosure Letter contradict each other.** The Update says Bluefen is "addressed", Riverlark will be "addressed" post-Completion, the Ironquay indemnity is "adequate", DD-006 is "not expected to be material" and the bonuses are "a matter for the Seller". The Disclosure Letter – the document that actually binds – admits that no Bluefen consent exists, Riverlark is unpaid with no discharge, Ironquay SOW3 is unpaid with no assignment, the privacy incident is unresolved, and the AUD 420,000 bonuses are missing from the funds flow. Treat the Update as advocacy; treat the Disclosure Letter as the factual record.

2. **The architecture is designed to convert every known DD issue into a non-claim.** General data-room disclosure (Sch 7) + constructive-knowledge bar (cl 8.3) + "all limitations apply to all Claims" (cl 12.3/13, 9.3/12.8/20.5) + fundamental warranties folded into the general regime means that, as drafted, virtually every item in the Disclosure Letter is disclosed against *and* barred by Buyer knowledge *and* capped at 20% *and* time-barred at 18 months. The combined effect is that Wattlebridge pays AUD 24m for a company with ~AUD 4.1m of identified unaddressed exposures and little contractual recourse.

The response should be structural, not piecemeal: (a) every identified DD issue becomes a condition precedent, a price/funds-flow adjustment, or a specific indemnity outside the limitation regime; and (b) the general limitation regime is rebuilt on orthodox NSW mid-market terms.

---

## Part A – The limitation and recourse architecture

### A1. Clause 12.1 – General cap at 20% (AUD 4.8m)
**Departure:** 20% is at the low end for a private AUD 24m sale with no W&I insurance and this volume of open issues. Twenty to thirty percent is seen in Australian deals, but normally where DD is clean or W&I sits on top.
**Push back:** Propose 50% as the opening position, with a floor of 30–35% if the Seller agrees to full carve-outs below. If the Seller will not move, make W&I (Seller-paid or cost-shared) or a retention the price of staying at 20%.

### A2. Clause 12.2 – De minimis AUD 25,000 and AUD 250,000 deductible basket
**Departure:** (i) The basket is a *deductible* ("only the excess"), not a tipping basket. (ii) AUD 25,000 per claim is high relative to the business's scale (c. AUD 12m revenue on the Bluefen 30% figure). (iii) No aggregation language – the three Sandbar AUD 110,000 renewals are a reminder that related matters get split.
**Push back:** Tipping basket (first-dollar recovery once exceeded); de minimis AUD 10,000–15,000; express aggregation of claims arising from the same or related facts; neither threshold to apply to fundamental, tax, or specific indemnity claims.

### A3. Clause 12.3/13 – 18-month claims period; "limitation applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise"
**Departure:** 18 months may not capture a full post-Completion audit cycle plus investigation. The default rule that every limitation applies to every Claim reverses the normal position and silently sweeps in indemnities, covenants and fundamental warranties.
**Push back:** 24 months for general warranties; 7 years for tax (aligned to ATO amendment periods, unlimited for fraud/evasion); fundamental and title warranties – 6 years minimum, preferably unlimited; specific indemnities – at least until the underlying matter is finally resolved plus 12 months. Replace the default with: *limitations apply only where expressly stated*.

### A4. Fundamental/title warranties subject to general caps and time limits
**Departure:** This is not "administrative simplicity"; it means that if Harbourglass does not actually own the shares, recovery is capped at AUD 4.8m on a AUD 24m purchase and barred after 18 months. Unacceptable in any market.
**Push back:** Title, capacity and authority warranties: cap 100% of price, no de minimis/basket, 6 years or unlimited, no disclosure against, no knowledge bar.

### A5. Clauses 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 – Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply to "all Claims of any nature"
**Departure:** As drafted this limits or excludes claims for fraud, wilful concealment, breach of pre-Completion covenants (gap, leakage, restraints), the specific indemnities, and the Seller's own Completion obligations.
**Push back:**
- Carve out fraud, dishonesty, wilful concealment and wilful default from every limitation (also note: under NSW law a contractual cap on fraud is unlikely to be enforced anyway, but don't rely on the court).
- Exclusive-remedy clause not to apply to indemnities, injunctive relief for restraints/confidentiality, or claims under the Completion mechanics.
- Non-reliance clause: accept a conventional acknowledgement but confirm it does not purport to exclude the Buyer's statutory rights (ACL s 18 cannot be contracted out of; a sweeping clause invites argument that the whole provision is unenforceable). Ensure the Disclosure Letter itself and the warranties are expressly carved out of "non-reliance".

### A6. Schedule 7 – General disclosure of the data room and "public registers"
**Departure:** Blanket data-room disclosure means every document in DD-002 to DD-012, however buried, qualifies every warranty. "Publicly searchable corporate records" is unbounded (ASIC, PPSR, court lists, IP registers, land titles – anywhere in Australia, at any date).
**Push back:**
- Replace with a **fair disclosure** standard: disclosed only if the fact, matter or circumstance is disclosed *in the Disclosure Letter* with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature, scope and likely effect of the matter.
- Public-records disclosure limited to a scheduled ASIC company search and PPSR search against the Company, each dated and attached.
- No disclosure against fundamental/title warranties, the tax indemnity, or the specific indemnities.
- Data room to be frozen, indexed and burned to USB, with the index attached. Note the cut-off was **22 September 2026 – over six weeks ago**. Require a bring-down and a prohibition on "updating" the disclosure letter at Completion except for matters arising after signing (with Buyer termination/indemnity rights if updates are material).

### A7. Clause 8.3 – Buyer "knowledge" bar including anything "discoverable" from the data room or public records
**Departure:** This is the most aggressive clause in the package. It imposes constructive knowledge of everything in the data room and the entire public record, and extends to advisers. Combined with A6, the Seller gets two bites: disclosed *and* known. Australian authority is not uniformly buyer-friendly on whether a buyer with actual knowledge of a breach can sue on a warranty, so this cannot be left ambiguous.
**Push back:**
- Delete. If any knowledge qualifier survives: actual knowledge only, of three named Wattlebridge individuals, of a matter *fairly disclosed in the Disclosure Letter*, and never applying to fundamental, tax or specific indemnity claims.
- Insert an affirmative clause: *the Buyer's rights are not affected by any investigation made by or on behalf of the Buyer, or by any knowledge of the Buyer or its advisers other than as fairly disclosed in the Disclosure Letter.*
- This is also why every known DD issue must be an **indemnity**, not a warranty: indemnities are not defeated by disclosure or knowledge.

### A8. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"
**Departure:** Paperbark is an analytics business – IP *is* the asset – and tax exposure runs on ATO timelines, not 18 months.
**Push back:** Separate tax indemnity (pre-Completion tax, 100% cap, 7 years, no disclosure against, Seller controls defence only with Buyer consent); IP warranties on ownership, chain of title (including contractor/employee assignments and moral-rights consents), no infringement, and open-source compliance, at a higher cap (suggest 50–100%) and 3–4 years.

### A9. Missing: security for claims
Nothing in the Seller package provides a source of recovery. Harbourglass Ventures is a "Ventures" vehicle; post-sale it may distribute proceeds. **Require** a retention/escrow (suggest AUD 2.4–3.6m, 10–15%, for 24 months, stepping down) or a parent/principal guarantee, or W&I insurance. Given the number of specific issues below, a retention is the cleanest solution and should be a priority ask.

---

## Part B – The specific DD issues

### B1. Bluefen (DD-002) – ~AUD 3.6m, ~30% of revenue; change-of-control consent not obtained
**Departure:** The Seller offers "reasonable endeavours" and proposes the CP is satisfied on delivery of "written consent" – but clause 11.3 attaches *conditions* to consent, none of which has been evidenced. A conditional consent that Bluefen can later rely on to terminate is worth little.
**Push back:**
- Condition precedent for the Buyer's sole benefit: Bluefen written consent, **unconditional or on conditions approved by the Buyer (acting reasonably)**, with evidence that any 11.3 conditions are satisfied, and confirmation that Bluefen will not exercise any termination/renegotiation right arising from the sale.
- Seller to use **best/all reasonable endeavours**, keep the Buyer informed and allow Buyer participation in discussions.
- Fallback if the Seller refuses a hard CP: price reduction or deferred consideration/earn-out tied to Bluefen retention through to [12] months post-Completion; at minimum, a revenue-loss indemnity outside the cap.
- Ask the Seller now whether Bluefen has been approached. The absence of anything in the data room six weeks after cut-off is itself a signal.

### B2. Riverlark Bank (DD-003) – ~AUD 3.2m outstanding; release "following Completion"
**Departure:** Directly contradicts the debt-free/cash-free basis. Clause 8.1 (change of control) is almost certainly an event of default on the share transfer, and clause 9.2 discharge will not occur until repayment. A post-Completion release leaves Wattlebridge owning a company in default with security over its assets (and possibly over the shares being bought – see B9).
**Push back:**
- Riverlark repaid **at Completion** out of the purchase price via the funds flow, against a bank payout letter (figure as at the Completion Date), executed deed of release, PPSR financing statement discharge (or signed discharge authority), and release of any share mortgage/guarantees – all as Completion deliverables.
- Expressly include the facility (principal, interest, break costs, fees) in the Debt/Net Debt definition and price adjustment. Prohibit further drawdowns between signing and Completion.
- If the bank cannot process the release on the day, releases go into escrow with the Seller's solicitors to be dated and delivered on receipt of funds – not "following Completion".

### B3. Closing bonuses (DD-005) – AUD 420,000 omitted from funds flow
**Departure:** "A matter for the Seller" is correct in principle but false in effect: the bonuses are payable *by the Company*, triggered *by Completion*, so they become the Buyer's cost the moment the shares transfer. The Seller is pocketing AUD 420,000 (plus on-costs) of the price.
**Push back:**
- Treat as a Seller transaction cost/Debt item: full AUD 420,000 **plus** superannuation (12% from 1 July 2025), NSW payroll tax (c. 5.45%), PAYG withholding compliance and any leave-loading effect – modelled at roughly AUD 495,000–500,000 all-in, subject to confirmation of whether the amounts are inclusive of super – deducted from the price or paid by the Seller into the Company at Completion.
- Clarify the "continued-employment" condition: if the bonus vests on Completion but is paid only on later continued service, the Seller still funds it (via price deduction or escrow); the Buyer should not inherit a retention cost it did not design.
- Confirm there are no other change-of-control triggers (options, phantom equity, accelerated vesting, good-leaver provisions) – request a full schedule, warranted.

### B4. Ironquay Development Studio (DD-004 / DD-010) – SOW3 IP conditional on payment; AUD 180,000 open; no assignment
**Departure:** Clause 7.3 means the Company **does not own** the SOW3 Project Materials until every SOW3 fee has cleared. If those materials are embedded in the Paperbark platform, Wattlebridge is buying a product it does not own. An indemnity "limited to the SOW3 payment" covers AUD 180,000, not the value of the IP, the cost of rebuilding it, or a third-party infringement claim.
**Push back:**
- Completion deliverable: evidence of cleared payment of all SOW3 (and SOW1/2) fees and an executed **confirmatory IP assignment** from Ironquay (including moral-rights consents from its personnel), or the Seller funds the AUD 180,000 through the funds flow and the Company pays at Completion with assignment delivered in escrow.
- Expand the indemnity to cover all loss arising from any defect in title to Ironquay deliverables, including re-development cost and third-party claims, uncapped or capped at 100% of price, outside basket/de minimis.
- Technical DD question for our team: what does SOW3 actually comprise and how embedded is it? That determines whether this is a AUD 180,000 problem or a core-asset problem.

### B5. Export/privacy incident (DD-006) – ~1,240 records sent to an unintended external address
**Departure:** The Seller calls it "preliminary" and "not expected to be material". The Disclosure Letter concedes that nobody yet knows whether the file was accessed, the scope, or whether notification is required. This is precisely the profile of an **eligible data breach** under Part IIIC of the Privacy Act 1988 (unauthorised disclosure of personal information likely to result in serious harm): the Company has a 30-day obligation to complete a reasonable and expeditious assessment and, if the test is met, notify the OAIC and affected individuals. Names, emails, roles and activity timestamps from what are presumably *customer* datasets also engage contractual data-protection obligations to those customers (quite possibly Bluefen) and the current civil-penalty regime (which now scales up to the greater of AUD 50m / 3x benefit / 30% turnover for serious interferences, plus the new mid-tier and infringement-notice penalties). The matter is also now **over six weeks old** – the 30-day assessment window has already run.
**Push back:**
- Pre-signing: demand the completed assessment, the incident log, confirmation of whether the recipient was contacted and deleted the file, whose data it was, and whether any customer contract required notification.
- Specific indemnity covering all loss from the incident (regulator penalties, notification costs, customer claims and credits, forensic/legal costs, contractual breach consequences), outside basket/de minimis, separate cap (suggest 100% of price), survival until resolution + limitation period, no disclosure or knowledge defence.
- Pre-Completion covenant: Seller to procure that the Company completes the assessment and any required notifications before Completion, in consultation with the Buyer; Buyer approval over any regulator/customer communication.
- Representation at Completion that no other security or privacy incidents have occurred (the governance question is what else this incident says about data handling in an analytics business).

### B6. Sandbar supplier renewals (DD-008 / DD-011) – 3 × AUD 110,000
**Departure:** The Seller asserts "ordinary course"; the Disclosure Letter admits it cannot say whether the renewals are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course. Three identical amounts from related documents, each sitting just above an AUD 100,000 line, invites the question whether they were structured to fall below a materiality or approval threshold.
**Push back:**
- Obtain the contracts; confirm term, termination rights, and whether services are needed post-Completion.
- If committed/accrued pre-Completion and not reflected in normalised working capital, include in Debt or adjust price. Ensure "ordinary course" in the pre-Completion conduct covenants and any locked-box leakage definition does not sweep in new multi-year commitments.
- Material-contract warranty threshold set so that related contracts are aggregated.

### B7. Office lease (DD-007) – notification obligation
Lower risk. Confirm the exact clause (notification vs consent vs landlord termination right), have the Seller give the notice pre-Completion and warrant compliance. Confirm no deemed assignment on change of control and no bank guarantee/security deposit to be replaced.

### B8. Mossvale (DD-009) – assignment restriction
The Seller's reading (share sale ≠ assignment) is probably right if the clause is a pure anti-assignment provision, but verify there is no "change of control" or "deemed assignment" limb and whether Mossvale has any practical leverage. If material, a comfort letter from Mossvale is cheap insurance.

### B9. Title (DD-012) – share register only
**Departure:** The share register is maintained by the Company (i.e., by the Seller). It is evidence, not proof. The Disclosure Letter is candid that the Buyer has not completed its own verification.
**Push back:** Our side to run a current ASIC company search (members, officers, charges history), PPSR search against the Company *and* Harbourglass, and review the constitution and any shareholders' agreement for pre-emptive rights, options or convertible instruments. Specifically check whether the Riverlark security package includes a mortgage over the Paperbark shares – that would need release at Completion (see B2). Title warranty to be absolute (A4), with a warranty that there are no options, rights or encumbrances over any shares.

### B10. Disclosure Letter clause 1.4 and clause 11
Non-admission wording (1.4) is standard and acceptable. Clause 11 is a useful admission: the Seller has not stated any conclusion about materiality or approval. Use it – it confirms nothing in the package should be read as a representation that any issue is resolved.

---

## Part C – Price and completion mechanics (cross-cutting)

On the Seller's own documents, the identified items that should come out of a "debt-free/cash-free" AUD 24m, or sit in indemnity/escrow, are:

| Item | Amount (AUD) | Proposed treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Riverlark facility | ~3,200,000 + interest/break costs | Repay at Completion from price; Debt |
| Closing bonuses + on-costs | ~420,000 + ~75,000–80,000 | Debt / Seller-funded |
| Ironquay SOW3 | 180,000 | Paid pre-Completion or Debt; assignment delivered |
| Sandbar renewals | 330,000 | Debt or WC, pending contract review |
| Privacy incident | unquantified | Specific indemnity + retention |
| Bluefen consent | ~3.6m revenue at risk | CP / deferred consideration |

Ensure the SPA's Debt/Net Debt and Transaction Costs definitions capture each of these expressly, and that the funds flow is a Completion deliverable the Buyer must approve.

---

## Summary of recommendations (priority order)

**Must-haves (walk-away items)**
1. Riverlark repaid and released **at** Completion; full inclusion in Debt.
2. Fundamental/title/capacity warranties: 100% cap, 6+ years, no disclosure, no knowledge bar.
3. Delete cl 8.3 constructive-knowledge bar; add "Buyer's investigation does not prejudice" clause.
4. Replace general data-room/public-record disclosure with a fair-disclosure standard tied to a frozen, indexed data room; no disclosure against fundamental/tax/specific-indemnity claims.
5. Specific indemnities (outside basket, de minimis and general cap) for: DD-006 privacy incident; Ironquay IP title; closing bonuses and on-costs; any Bluefen loss if the Seller refuses a hard CP.
6. Bluefen consent as a Buyer-benefit CP, unconditional or on Buyer-approved conditions, with evidence of cl 11.3 satisfaction.
7. Retention/escrow (10–15%, 24 months) or W&I/guarantee.

**Strong pushes**
8. General cap to 50% (floor 30–35%); tipping basket; lower de minimis; claim aggregation.
9. 24-month general period; 7 years tax; separate tax indemnity; enhanced IP warranties.
10. Limitations apply only where expressly stated; carve out fraud, wilful concealment, covenants, indemnities and Completion obligations from cl 9.3/12.8/20.5 and the exclusive-remedy clause.
11. AUD 420,000 bonuses (grossed up for super/payroll tax) into the funds flow as a Seller cost.
12. Ironquay fees paid and confirmatory assignment delivered as a Completion deliverable.

**Diligence actions on our side (this week)**
13. Independent ASIC/PPSR searches (Company and Seller), constitution review, confirm any share security to Riverlark.
14. Demand the completed DD-006 breach assessment and incident log; assess NDB-scheme and customer-contract notification positions.
15. Obtain Sandbar, Mossvale and lease documents; confirm termination rights and change-of-control language.
16. Technical review of what SOW3 Project Materials comprise and how embedded they are in the platform.
17. Require a bring-down of the data room and Disclosure Letter from 22 September 2026 to a date proximate to signing.

I can turn any of these into mark-up language for the SPA or a response letter to Harbourglass's counsel on request.
=== END ADVICE ===
